newsitem.title: USA: Occidental Pete abandons Sudan interest.
newsitem.headline: Occidental Pete abandons Sudan interest.

text.p: With the recent awards of two major oil production sharing agreements in Sudan to non-U.S. companies, California-based Occidental Petroleum Corp is no longer interested in Sudan.
"There are no other active projects in Sudan," said Occidental President Dale Laurance.

The company had long sought a stake in a major oil field in the African nation, but the Sudanese goverment excluded the company from an award with Arakis Energy Corp last December which went instead to Malaysia's state oil company Petronas, and China National Petroleum Corp.
Occidental recently withdrew from a another potential venture with Canada's International Petroleum Corp, which Thursday signed an oil sharing agreement with Sudan.
"We walked away from those transactions for economic reasons," Laurance told Reuters, after speaking at a meeting of the Moscow International Petroleum Club here.

He said a Washington Post story last month that implied that the Clinton administration had given Occidental a special exemption from regulations barring transactions between U.S. companies and governments accused of sponsoring terrorism, including Sudan, had not figured in the company's decisions.
In a letter to the Washington Post published Friday but written on January 24, Occidental said it had sought no special exemptions from the administration.

The regulations issued last August were designed to block deals that might help government-backed terrorists. But it allowed business deals to go ahead in Sudan and Syria while banning all business in Cuba, Iran, Iraq, Libya, and North Korea, against which Washington already had broad sanctions.
Lawmakers hauled in administration officials recently to explain why the rules were looser for Sudan and Syria, a spokesman for the Senate Foreign Relations Committee said.
"We're hoping the administration's going to correct it," said Marc Thiessen, the committee spokesman.
"Clearly in writing these regulations, they misread congressional intent," he said.
He said House and Senate aides told the administration: "Correct it, or we will." However they did not set any deadline for the administration.
State Department officials have repeatedly said they believed Congress had not intended to curb legitimate business deals, but wanted to cut off funds that might be funneled toward terrorists.
